apace.e: From Middle English apās (“step by step, slowly; quickly, rapidly; at once, promptly”), from Old French à pas (“at a quick pace”).

apart.e: From Middle English apart, aparte, a-part, a part, from Anglo-Norman a part, from Latin ad partem (“to the side”).
apart.g: Placed separately (in regard to space or time).

ape.e: From Middle English ape, from Old English apa (“ape, monkey”), from Proto-West Germanic *apō, from Proto-Germanic *apô (“monkey, ape”), possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ep- (“water”), compare Proto-Celtic *abū (“river”) (hence English place name Avon, Irish abha, Welsh afon), if the word originally referred to a "water sprite".
ape.g: An anthropoid of the superfamily Hominoidea, generally larger than monkeys and distinguished from them by having no tail.

apiece.e: Univerbation of a + piece (noun), from Late Middle English a pece. Pece is derived from Anglo-Norman pece, peece, peice, Middle French piece, and Old French pece, pice, piece (“part of a whole”) (modern French pièce); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Late Latin *pettia, *pettium (compare pecia, pecium, petia, petium (“broken piece, fragment.
apiece.g: Following a noun or noun phrase: by, for, or to each one; each by itself.

apostasy.e: From Latin apostasia, from Ancient Greek ἀποστασία (apostasía, “defection, revolt”), from ἀφίστημι (aphístēmi, “to withdraw, revolt”), from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).
apostasy.g: The renunciation of a belief or set of beliefs.

apostle.e: From Middle English apostle, from Old French apostle, from Late Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos, “one sent forth, apostle”). Merged with Old English apostol, borrowing from the same Latin source.
apostle.g: A missionary, or leader of a religious mission, especially one in the early Christian Church (but see Apostle).
apostle.sf: From Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos, “one sent forth, apostle”)

apothecary.e: From Old French apotecaire (whence French apothicaire), from Medieval Latin apothēcārius (“storekeeper”), from Latin apothēca (“(originally) repository, storehouse, warehouse; (later) shop, store”) + -ārius (occupational suffix), from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “a repository, storehouse”).
apothecary.g: Synonym of pharmacist: a person who sells medicine, especially (historical) one who made and sold their own medicines in the medieval or ear

apparent.e: From Middle English apparaunt, aparaunt, from Old French aparent, aparant, in turn from Latin appārēns, appārentis, present participle of appāreō.
apparent.g: Capable of being seen, or easily seen; open to view; visible to the eye; within sight or view.

appeal.e: From Middle English apel, appel (“formal accusation brought in court; a challenge to trial by combat; an appeal to a higher court or authority; plea (for mercy, protection, etc.); pealing (of bells)”), from Old French apel (“a call”) (modern French appel (“a call; an appeal”)), from apeler (“to call; to call out”).
appeal.g: An application to a superior court or judge for a decision or order by an inferior court or judge to be reviewed and overturned.

appeal.e: From Middle English apelen, appelen (“to accuse; to make a formal charge before a court, etc., impeach; to challenge to trial by combat; to apply to a higher court or authority for review of a decision; to call upon for a decision, favour, help, etc.; to call by a name”), from Old French apeler (“to call; to call out”); see further at etymology 1.
appeal.g: Often followed by against (the inferior court's decision) or to (the superior court): to apply to a superior court or judge for a decision o

appear.e: From Middle English apperen, aperen, borrowed from Old French aparoir (French apparoir), from Latin appāreō (“to appear”), from ad (“to”) + pāreō (“to come forth, to become visible”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-s- (“watch, see”), s-present of *peh₂- (“protect”).
appear.g: To come or be in sight; to be in view; to become visible.

appearance.e: Borrowed from Middle French apparence, from Latin apparentia, from appareo. Morphologically appear + -ance.
appearance.g: The act of appearing or coming into sight; the act of becoming visible to the eye.

appease.e: From Middle English apesen, from Old French apeser (“to pacify, bring to peace”).
appease.g: To make quiet; to calm; to reduce (something) to a state of peace; to dispel (anger, hatred, etc.).

appertain.e: From Middle English apperteinen, apertenen, borrowed from Old French apartenir (French appartenir), from Late Latin appertinēre, from ad (“to”) + Latin pertinēre (“to reach to, belong”).
appertain.g: To belong to or be a part of, whether by right, nature, appointment, or custom; to relate to.

appetite.e: From Middle English appetit, from Old French apetit (French appétit), from Latin appetitus, from appetere (“to strive after, long for”); ad + petere (“to seek”).
appetite.g: A desire to eat food or consume drinks.

applaud.e: From Middle English applauden, from Latin applaudere (“to clap the hands together, applaud”), from ad (“to”) + plaudere (“to strike, clap”).

apple.e: It may have come to be identified with the apple because of the similarity between Latin mālum (“apple”) and malum (“evil; misery, torment; wrongdoing”). The inheritance from Germanic is clear, but the etymology of the word beyond that point is uncertain and disputed.
apple.g: A common, firm, round fruit produced by a tree of the genus Malus.

apples.e: From Cockney rhyming slang apples and pears. (nice): From Australian rhyming slang apples and spice or apples and rice.
apples.g: Clipping of apple and pears or apples and pears (“stairs”).

apply.e: From Middle English aplien, borrowed from Old French applier, from Latin applicō, from ad- + plicō (“fold; arrive”).
apply.g: To lay or place; to put (one thing to another)

appoint.e: From Middle English apointen, borrowed from Old French apointier (“to prepare, arrange, lean, place”) (French appointer (“to give a salary, refer a cause”)), from Late Latin appunctō (“to bring back to the point, restore, to fix the point in a controversy, or the points in an agreement”); Latin ad + punctum (“a point”).
appoint.g: To set, fix or determine (a time or place for something such as a meeting, or the meeting itself) by authority or agreement.

appointment.e: From Middle English appoyntement, apoyntement, from Old French appointement, equivalent to appoint + -ment.
appointment.g: The act of appointing a person to hold an office or to have a position of trust.

apportion.e: From Middle French apportionner, from Old French aporcioner, from Late Latin apportionare, from Latin ad + portio. By surface analysis, ap- + portion.
apportion.g: To divide and distribute portions of a whole.

appraise.e: From Middle English apreisen, from Old French aprisier (“apraise, set a price on”) (compare modern French apprécier), from Late Latin appretiare, from ad- + Latin pretium (“price, value”) (English precious), from which also appreciate, a doublet.
appraise.g: To determine the value or worth of (something), particularly as a person appointed for this purpose.

appraise.e: Form of apprise in use since 1706 but considered incorrect by some.

appreciation.e: From French appréciation. By surface analysis, appreciate + -ion.

apprehend.e: From Late Middle English apprehenden (“to grasp, take hold of; to comprehend; to learn”), from Old French apprehender (modern French appréhender (“to apprehend; to catch; to dread”)), from Latin apprehendere, adprehendere, the present active infinitive of apprehendō, adprehendō (“to grab, grasp, seize, take; to apprehend, arrest; to comprehend, understand.
apprehend.g: To be or become aware of (something); to perceive.

approach.e: From Middle English aprochen, borrowed from Old French aprochier (modern French approcher), from Late Latin appropiāre, a verb based on Latin prope (“near”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pro- (a variant of *per- (“before, in front; first”)) + *-kʷe (“suffix forming distributives from interrogatives”)).
approach.g: To come or go near, in place or time; to move toward; to advance nearer; to draw nigh.

approach.e: From Middle English approche (“approach, arrival”), from approchen, aprochen (“to come or go near, approach; to adjoin, be close by; to enter (someone’s) presence; to be or become involved; to reach (a certain state); to arrive; to befall, happen to; to become similar to, resemble; to be a match for (someone)”); see etymology 1.
approach.g: An act of drawing near in place or time; an advancing or coming near.

approve.e: From Middle English aproven, appreoven, appreven, apreven, borrowed from Old French aprover, approver, approuvir, appreuver (“to approve”), from Latin approbō, from ad + probō (“to esteem as good, approve, prove”). By surface analysis, ad- + prove.
approve.g: To officially sanction; to ratify; to confirm; to set as satisfactory.

approve.e: From Middle English approuen, approven, from Old French aprouer; a- + a form apparently derived from the pro, prod, in Latin prōsum (“be useful or profitable”).
approve.g: To make profit of; to convert to one's own profit — said especially of waste or common land appropriated by the lord of the manor.

apron.e: Rebracketing of napron (a napron → an apron), from Middle English naperoun, napron, apron, from Old French napperon, diminutive of nappe (“tablecloth”), from Latin mappa (“napkin”). For other similar cases of rebracketing, see adder, daffodil, newt, nickname, orange, trickle, umpire.
apron.g: An article of clothing worn over the front of the torso and/or legs for protection from spills; also historically worn by Freemasons and as

apt.e: From Old French apte, from Latin aptus (“suitable, fitting”). Either from obsolete apere (“to fasten, to join, to fit”), akin to apisci (“to reach, attain”) (compare with Greek ἅπτειν (áptein, “to fasten”) and Sanskrit आप्त (āpta, “fit”), from आप् (āp, “to reach, attain”)) or from *h₂ep- (“to join, fit (in)”).
apt.g: Suitable; appropriate; fit or fitted; suited.
